item.title: Anthony Constantino’s Post-Election Crashout
item.description:
At an election eve rally in upstate New York, Republican congressional candidate Anthony Constantino told the crowd he had a dramatic announcement: Donald Trump was wrong about one thing. An audible gasp rippled through the converted airplane hangar. What could it possibly be? “Fake news” wasn’t accurate, Constantino said. “It’s actually evil news.” The candidate went on to gesture at the press pen and tell the crowd to take photos of its nefarious inhabitants. The campaign had not granted me credentials, so, like everyone else, I turned my attention to the people Constantino said “should be ashamed” of themselves. What Constantino did not seem to realize was that the most embarrassing thing about the event was that it was happening at all. item.title: Kenyan cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison
item.description:
A Kenyan doomsday cult leader was sentenced Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people after ordering followers to starve themselves to meet Jesus. Pastor Paul Mackenzie was sentenced by Kenya’s High Court in the coastal city of Mombasa after being convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult, according to the Associated Press. He received two consecutive 100-year terms: one for murders by starvation and another for murders by direct homicide. Justice Diana Kavedza said Mackenzie, the leader of the Good News International Church, bore the “primary criminal culpability” for leading his followers into an isolated area and directing them to starve themselves to death, the outlet reported. “The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law,” the judge added. At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers. item.title: Europe bomb hoaxes widen
item.description:
The series of hoax bomb scares sent to several Irish media outlets and European airlines are likely part of a coordinated campaign of disruption, according to the Irish government. Dozens of commercial flights have been targetted by email with threats said to be over and above the typical hoax in specificty. Ireland's broadcaster RTE who's staff evacuated the premises this morning and several Italian airlines, say they received a mesage cliaming to be from a Russian extremist group calling itself the Fighters of the Male State, which denied its implication. France 24's Jean-Emile Jammine speaks to Eric Schouten, founder and CEO of Dyami Security Intelligence.

item.title: Democrats take control of Georgia’s powerful utility regulator
item.description:
Beginning in January, three of the five officials on the Georgia Public Service Commission will be Democrats. It will be the first time the party has controlled the powerful energy regulation board in 30 years. The commission, which regulates utilities including the state’s largest electric provider, Georgia Power, has come under more scrutiny in recent years due to rising power bills and the high energy demands of data centers. Now, Democrats plan to focus on affordability, clean energy, and closer scrutiny of Georgia Power. “There’s a long laundry list of things that need to be looked into,” said Democratic Commissioner Peter Hubbard, who won his reelection bid this week. “And so we’ll have to triage, in fact, and decide how best to move forward.” One of his first priorities will be launching an affordability docket, he said — a series of hearings that would delve into the reasons for…

item.title: Seeds and preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
item.description:
Small changes in how parts of the brain communicate with one another can help predict a person’s likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease years before any memory lapses appear, according to a study published in Science Advances. Stanford Medicine researchers used brain scans and a computer model to look for early clues about why some older adults develop memory and thinking problems while others stay sharp. Investigators examined resting brain scans from two opposing groups: patients diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and older individuals known as "super agers," whose memory capabilities match people decades younger. item.title: California’s new teen social media law challenged in court by Meta, TikTok and Google
item.description:
In summary California’s ban on addictive social media features for kids takes effect in January. Now Big Tech is trying to stop it in federal court. Tech giants Meta, Google, and TikTok are suing to block a landmark California law meant to protect kids’ mental health on social media platforms. The law, one of a slate of bills signed by Gov. Newsom this year to protect kids online, would block social media companies from offering “addictive” features to teens under 16. Set to go into effect in January, the law defines addictive features as design choices like infinite scroll, autoplay, and recommendations. Those features are blamed in part for a teen mental health crisis, which the law seeks to curb. item.title: Trump’s Triumphal Arch Hits a Blue Wall
item.description:
Americans overwhelmingly despise President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot high “triumphal arch.” More than 100,000 people submitted written comments to the Interior Department, most opposing its placement near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery. With its “eternal flame,” the golden winged figure on top, and now possibly snipers and a munitions dump for its alleged “national security” importance, the arch has even been compared to Nazi monuments . No matter. Trump had threatened to begin construction on the arch as soon as the now Trump-aligned National Capital Planning Commission held its final vote approving it, which it did late Thursday night. His hand-picked majority said the digging should start, and almost immediately after the decision, US District Court Judge Tanya S. Chutkan said the digging should stop. item.title: Latino voters propel Democrats to big wins with leftward swing
item.description:
AUSTIN — Texas. Florida. Pennsylvania. Colorado. Arizona. Nevada. California. The historic landslide of Latino voters toward Democrats hit battleground after battleground Tuesday, crumbling the coalition that helped carry President Donald Trump to victory just one cycle ago. “This is an earthquake,” Democratic Latino operative Sergio Gonzalez told POLITICO on the sidelines of Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s victory party in Austin. “Latinos were angry.
